Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: For a civilian assault trauma, 'talks about military' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless the assault specifically involved military context, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. It is not supported by the other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'I feel guilty for surviving when others did not' implies a trauma involving deaths of others or a mass-casualty context. That does not cohere with the rest of this profile, which otherwise describes an individual assault without any indication that others were killed.

issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: This appraisal is the main incoherent item in the profile. The rest of the report is organized around fear, betrayal, hypervigilance, male-related/interpersonal triggers, and fragmented sensory trauma memory after assault. In contrast, fearing that she will lose control of her own rage and do something terrible introduces a perpetration/anger-control theme that is not supported by the triggers, threat items, or memory content. It does not fit the dominant cognitive formulation in which negative appraisals feed threat and memory; the other appraisal items plausibly amplify fear and mistrust, but this one points to a different clinical concern not otherwise represented in the profile. Given the otherwise tightly fear-based assault presentation, this item is hard to integrate clinically with the selected set.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: This threat item is the least coherent element in the profile. The rest of the selected triggers, appraisals, and memory items consistently describe an interpersonal assault formulation centered on men, betrayal, mistrust, conversational/emotional triggers, and trauma memories. By contrast, needing to stay alert at night implies a more generalized ongoing danger-monitoring pattern that is not specifically supported by the selected triggers or appraisals. It is not impossible in PTSD, but here it fits less well than the other threat items and is weakly linked to the formulation, especially because Threat has no active edge to Maladaptive Strategies and the profile lacks other nighttime/sleep-related material.

vignette: Sophie is a 54-year-old European-American woman who works as a chef at a bustling downtown restaurant. She is married and has been coming to therapy after experiencing significant distress following an assault that occurred several months ago. Sophie's traumatic experience has left her with complex reactions that have affected both her personal life and professional duties. The incident took place in the early evening when she was closing up her restaurant kitchen. A former coworker, who had recently lost his job and become unstable, broke into the building through a back door that hadn't been properly secured. He confronted Sophie, brandishing a knife and demanding money. The encounter was chaotic; Sophie remembers flashes of movement, the sound of her own heartbeat pounding in her ears, and the overwhelming fear as she tried to protect herself. The assailant eventually fled, but the event left Sophie with lasting psychological scars. In the months following the assault, Sophie has experienced a range of symptoms that have profoundly impacted her life. She finds certain conversation topics incredibly distressing; any mention of security vulnerabilities or violent incidents can send her into a state of anxiety and panic. Emotional closeness with others has also become difficult for her. Being in close relationships now triggers feelings of unease and vulnerability, especially when she is alone with men, whom she perceives as potential threats. Sophie's hypervigilance has manifested in various ways. In the kitchen, where sudden movements are common, she often reacts sharply to unexpected actions from colleagues, jumping up at the slightest noise or motion. Her heightened state of alertness extends beyond work; even in ordinary situations, such as walking down a street or sitting in a restaurant, strangers approaching her can set off a cascade of fear and anxiety. Her memory of the traumatic event remains fragmented. Sophie struggles to articulate the sequence of events, instead recalling disjointed images and sensations. When memories surface, she experiences bodily reenactments-feeling physically as though she is back in that moment of terror, with her body mimicking the tense postures and rapid heart rate. Sophie's negative appraisals have become deeply ingrained beliefs. She has come to believe that there are no safe spaces or trustworthy people. The betrayal by a former coworker who had once been part of her professional family has left her feeling profoundly mistrustful. Even in everyday interactions, she is certain that anyone could be a potential threat. Sophie's occupational environment, particularly the kitchen setting where sudden movements and close physical proximity are constant, has become increasingly difficult to navigate. Her reactions have sometimes caused friction with coworkers who perceive her as overly reactive or paranoid. This has led to strained relationships at work, further exacerbating her sense of isolation and mistrust. What finally brought Sophie to therapy was a combination of escalating anxiety at work and mounting relational stress at home. She had become increasingly isolated from her husband, whom she loved dearly but now found it difficult to be emotionally close with. Her fear of harm and deep-seated mistrust were starting to erode the intimacy they once shared. In therapy, Sophie is most afraid of being re-victimized and losing the relationships that mean the most to her. She hopes to regain a sense of safety and trust in both her personal and professional life. Through this process, she aims to learn how to manage her distressing symptoms and rebuild her confidence in navigating everyday situations without constant fear and hypervigilance.
